g-voice-05.reason: Subject is 'twelve' (of the technicians); the technicians receive places, so passive 'were offered'. 'offered' (active) makes technicians the givers; the nearer noun 'plant' tempts it but cannot be the subject. 'have offered' and 'offering' fail on meaning/finite form.
g-voice-05.ldbs: L yes (plant offered places reads fine); D yes (subject 'twelve' ~20 words back); B yes (nearest-noun/plant-as-agent pull to active simple past); S yes (strip 'who applied ... plant' to find subject, then judge voice).
g-voice-05.why: L, D, B, S all fail: active 'offered' passes the window and the real subject sits behind a long relative clause.

g-voice-06.reason: Gerund after 'without' takes the shipment as its implied subject; a shipment is opened by others, so 'being opened' (+ 'even once'). 'opening' would need customs officers as agent, but they are not the main-clause subject (dangling), so an editor would not pass it; 'having opened' and 'to be opened' are ungrammatical after 'without'.
g-voice-06.ldbs: L yes ('without opening even once' reads fine); D yes (subject 'shipment' 11+ words back); B yes (the last clause supplies 'customs officers' as a tempting agent for active 'opening'); S yes (identify the gerund's implied subject, then choose voice).
g-voice-06.why: All four fail; 'opening' survives the window and is pulled by the later 'customs officers'.
g-voice-06.editorNote: Active 'opening' is a dangling gerund (agent only in a relative clause at the end); editors would reject it, so treated as a legitimate trap, not ambiguity. Borderline hard/medium: if a reviewer judges B weak, it is medium.

g-mandative-05.reason: 'demanded ... that every airline ______' calls for the bare (mandative) form 'complete'. 'completed' would need past reference, contradicting 'within sixty days' and 'has demanded'; 'to complete' and 'completing' are ungrammatical after 'that + subject'.
g-mandative-05.ldbs: L yes ('aircraft completed'/'aircraft to complete' read fine in the window); D yes ('demanded that' ~9 words before the gap); B yes ('completed' as past tense agreeing with singular 'airline'; 'to complete' by demand-someone-to pattern); S yes (find real subject 'every airline' past 'more than fifty aircraft', then recognise mandative).
g-mandative-05.why: L, D, B, S: the that-clause cue sits outside the window and plural 'aircraft' sits right before the gap.

g-mandative-06.reason: 'asked ... that no resident be evicted' is mandative subjunctive. 'to be' is ungrammatical after 'that no resident'; 'being' and 'been' lack a finite form.
g-mandative-06.ldbs: L no: 'that no resident' is inside the four-word window, so 'to be' fails locally and 'being'/'been' fail too; the only finite form is 'be'. D partly (asked is far) but not needed; B no; S no.
g-mandative-06.why: L fails: no distractor survives the window because 'that' + subject sits right before the gap.
g-mandative-06.fix: Strictly easy by 3.4. To raise it, put a modifier between 'no resident' and the gap (e.g. 'no resident of the estate, whatever the arrears,') so that 'to be' survives locally. Do not add 'is/was' as a distractor: British formal accepts the indicative after 'asked that', which would be ambiguous.
g-mandative-06.editorNote: Borderline medium only for learners who do not know the subjunctive; by the 3.4 test it is easy.

g-conditional-05.reason: Inverted third conditional: 'Had the manager ... been told'. 'If ... been told' lacks the auxiliary; 'Should' and 'Were' do not take 'been told' in a past-unreal clause.
g-conditional-05.ldbs: L yes ('If the ... manager' reads fine); D yes ('been told' ~13 words after the gap, behind a relative clause); B no (good students notice 'been' with no 'had' once they read it); S borderline (relative clause contains 'had handled', a mild attractor, but no agreement/subject decision depends on it).
g-conditional-05.why: L and D fail; B no, so medium. S is borderline and I did not count it.
g-conditional-05.editorNote: Borderline hard on S; stayed strict at medium.

g-conditional-06.reason: Past counterfactual: 'if the permit had not been suspended' needs main clause 'would have opened'. 'would open' is present/future; 'had opened' and 'opened' are wrong main-clause forms for an unreal past (British and American alike).
g-conditional-06.ldbs: L yes (would open/had opened/opened all read fine in the window); D yes (if-clause at the end, ~15 words after the gap); B no (a mid-high learner will not confidently choose the wrong forms once the if-clause is read); S no.
g-conditional-06.why: L and D fail, B and S pass: clue at sentence end, like g-tense-06, which is medium.

g-parallel-05.reason: 'must either book ... or obtain': bare verb parallel to 'book' after 'must'. 'to obtain', 'obtaining', 'obtained' break the parallel; no standard-written reading accepts 'must either book ... or to obtain'.
g-parallel-05.ldbs: L yes (all four read fine after 'January, or'); D yes ('must either book' ~15 words back); B partly ('to obtain' as plausible purpose infinitive); S yes (skip the 'whose rates ...' insertion to find the parallel partner 'book').
g-parallel-05.why: L, D, S fail (B partial): the parallel partner is behind a whose-clause.
g-parallel-05.editorNote: Confidence 4: borderline hard/medium because 'must either' flags the parallelism.

g-parallel-06.reason: 'Both X and Y' needs 'and'. 'as well as' after 'Both' is condemned by usage guides (editors correct it), 'along with' and 'or' do not complete 'Both'.
g-parallel-06.ldbs: L yes ('on the third, as well as / and the three smaller ...' read fine); D yes ('Both' ~22 words back); B weak (both...and is universally known; 'as well as' is a weak temptation); S no.
g-parallel-06.why: L and D fail; B weak, so medium.
g-parallel-06.fix: The clue is the sentence-initial correlative 'Both' (textbook signal at the start, 1.1 / 3.5). Move 'Both' mid-sentence (e.g. 'Notice was given that both the main library, ... and ...') or switch to a neither/nor or either/or frame.
g-parallel-06.editorNote: 'both ... as well as' is attested but corrected by editors; kept as a legitimate trap, not ambiguity.

g-quantity-06.reason: 'equipment' is uncountable and takes singular 'is', so 'Much of the ... equipment is'. 'Many' and 'Several' need a plural countable; 'Few' needs a countable plural.
g-quantity-06.ldbs: L yes (Many/Several/Few of the newly ordered ... read fine in the window); D yes ('equipment' is the 7th word after the gap); B no (uncountable 'equipment' is well known, like less/fewer); S weak (find head noun behind modifiers).
g-quantity-06.why: L and D fail; B no, so medium.
g-quantity-06.fix: Lowercase all four options (Many, Several, Much, Few are capitalised mid-sentence after a comma, which looks like a formatting leftover).
g-quantity-06.editorNote: Options are capitalised although the gap is mid-sentence.

g-compare-06.reason: 'as high as that [= the fee] for spaces ...': singular 'fee' needs 'that'. 'those' would need a plural 'fees' antecedent that is not in the sentence (nearest plurals 'structures', 'garages' are not what is compared); 'it for spaces' and 'them' are ungrammatical.
g-compare-06.ldbs: L yes ('as high as those for spaces in the new garages' reads fine); D yes (antecedent 'fee' ~20 words back); B yes ('those' pulled by plural 'structures/garages'); S yes (find head 'fee' past 'charged for permits ... most of which were renovated').
g-compare-06.why: L, D, B, S all fail.

g-participle-08.reason: 'Patients arriving ... after 5 p.m. ... will be seen' is a reduced relative; the main verb is 'will be seen'. 'arrive', 'have arrived', 'are arriving' would create a second finite verb with no conjunction.
g-participle-08.ldbs: L yes ('Patients arrive at the Rosewood Clinic' reads fine); D yes (main verb 'will be seen' ~20 words after the gap); B yes (a subject without a verb pulls toward a finite form); S yes (spot the real predicate, then see the participle as a reduced relative).
g-participle-08.why: L, D, B, S all fail.
g-participle-08.editorNote: Very familiar TOEIC pattern (arriving after ...), but not marked tooClose.

g-relative-07.reason: Relative pronoun is the subject of 'has' (parenthetical 'the review panel decides'), so 'whoever'. 'whomever' is the over-correction (4.2); 'who' and 'whom' cannot follow 'to' without -ever.
g-relative-07.ldbs: L yes ('to whomever the review panel' reads fine); D yes ('has' ~6 words after the gap); B yes (over-correction after 'to'); S yes (see through the parenthetical to the subject role).
g-relative-07.why: L, D, B, S all fail.

g-agree-07.reason: Inverted sentence: the subject is plural 'plans', so 'are'. 'is' is pulled by the singular 'agreement', 'Friday' and 'portfolio'; 'has been' is singular; 'being' lacks a finite verb.
g-agree-07.ldbs: L yes ('on Friday, is the original signed' reads fine); D yes (subject 'plans' is the 5th word after the gap); B yes (attraction to 'agreement'); S yes (spot the inversion, find the subject after the gap).
g-agree-07.why: L, D, B, S all fail.

g-prep-10.reason: 'adhere to'. 'with' (comply with) and 'by' (abide by) are blends; 'for' is wrong.
g-prep-10.ldbs: L yes ('without exception, with/by the security protocols' read fine); D yes ('adhere' ~13 words before); B weak (good learners know 'adhere to'); S no.
g-prep-10.why: L and D fail; B weak, so medium.
g-prep-10.editorNote: 'adhere by' appears occasionally but editors correct it; treated as a legitimate trap, no fix needed.

overall: No ambiguous items; no mustFix. Bands: hard 8 (voice-05, voice-06, mandative-05, parallel-05, compare-06, participle-08, relative-07, agree-07), medium 5 (conditional-05, conditional-06, parallel-06, quantity-06, prep-10), easy 1 (mandative-06). Hard share 57%, above the 30% target; easy share 7%; easier-than-TOEIC 1/14. Weak spots: g-mandative-06 is easy because 'that no resident' sits inside the window; g-parallel-06 puts the clue in the sentence-initial 'Both'; g-quantity-06 has capitalised options in a mid-sentence gap. voice-06 and parallel-05 are borderline hard/medium. Single-answer quality is strong; business register and sentence shapes resemble real Part 5. Unit repetition within batch: two voice, two mandative, two conditional, two parallel items use distinct sub-types.
